title: Goodness, justice, truth; prove what pleases; expose darkness (Eph 5:9–17)
english: You will also bring them up short with the fact that Christ is justice. Goodness shows itself in doing good; justice in giving each what he deserves; and truth in knowing the reason of all things.

"Testing what is pleasing to the Lord" (Ephesians 5:10). We need to do everything with deliberation, so that, looking closely at each thing to be done and examining it, we may accept, like approved money changers, what passes the test and pleases God, and shake off what fails the test and displeases him. Since the phrasing is left hanging, it seems to me it could be restored like this: "Do not, then, become fellow partakers with them, testing what is pleasing to the Lord. Even if you were once darkness, now, being light in the Lord, walk as children of light, showing the fruits of the light in all goodness and justice and truth."

"And take no part in the fruitless works of darkness" (Ephesians 5:11). Elsewhere too he gave the name "fruit" to what belongs to the Spirit and "work" to what belongs to the flesh, when he said, "Now the works of the flesh are plain: they are fornication" and the rest, "but the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace" and the rest (Galatians 5:19-22). Here, though, he says that the works of darkness are fruitless, and the one who does them takes part in them.

"But rather expose them" (Ephesians 5:11). Exposing, too, must be counted among the commandments. It will be done by the one who would not hear, "Hypocrite, first take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye" (Matthew 7:5). That is why the prophets, who were in no way open to reproof themselves, reproved those who sinned.

"For the things done by them in secret are shameful even to speak of" (Ephesians 5:12). By whom? He has not said quite clearly beforehand, unless one refers the phrase to the sons of disobedience, so that it reads: "For the things done in secret by the sons of disobedience are shameful even to speak of." And those things were fornication and uncleanness.

"But all things, when they are exposed by the light, are made plain; for everything that is made plain is light. Therefore it says, 'Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you'" (Ephesians 5:13-14). Origen says: Since the works of darkness, once exposed, are made plain by the light, as the things exposed are changed into light, it is said to those who are asleep and lie in deadness because they have done the fruitless works of darkness, "Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you."

Someone might ask who it is that speaks in what is written here, "Therefore it says, Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead." One will say that the apostle read these words in one of the prophets and wrote them down here. Another will say that the apostle himself is giving a voice to words spoken by the Spirit, to urge people toward repentance.

You will ask, further, how the same person is told "Awake, sleeper," as one who is alive and asleep, and "Rise from the dead," as one who has died. Perhaps, then, it is this: there is the spirit of the man that is in him, which we have observed is spoken of as the better part; and there is something second, the soul, which can receive both sickness and death from sins. So "Awake, sleeper" is said because of the spirit, and "Rise from the dead" because of the soul; for "the soul that sins, it shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4), but nowhere have we found a death of the spirit. And Christ, being the true light, will shine on the one who is roused from sleep and has risen from the dead.

"See, then, that you walk carefully, not as unwise but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is" (Ephesians 5:15-17). Origen says: Whoever tests, in each thing he says and does and thinks, what is pleasing to the Lord will also be able, from close attention, to see carefully how he is to walk; and whoever sees carefully how he is to walk is wise in every way. And since some have a fairly good intention, yet, not being wise, want to see carefully how they walk, he added, "not as unwise but as wise." For to see carefully, even in matters of conduct, is the work of wisdom.

"Redeeming the time, because the days are evil." As if buying the time for yourselves, time that holds evil days as far as human life goes. When we spend the time on something needful, then, we have bought it and bought it back for ourselves, as though it had been sold to human wickedness. title: Redeeming evil days; wine and Spirit; psalms; thanks; mutual submission (Eph 5:16–21)
english: needful and on gaining the blessed life. And when we redeem the time that lies in evil days, we change the evil days, as it were, into good ones; for ourselves we make them, as it were, not evil days of the present age but good days of the age to come.

"Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is" (Ephesians 5:17). "Therefore": because of what? Is it that, because you are to look carefully how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, you must not become foolish? For if you are foolish, you will not walk carefully, nor as the wise do. He commands them to search out the will of the Lord and to understand it, so that wherever they grasp something about what they should do, they may do it as the Lord's will, and wherever they suffer, they may bear it as something that happens by the Lord's will.

"And do not get drunk with wine, in which is debauchery, but be filled in spirit" (Ephesians 5:18). Origen says: These words can be understood quite simply, since debauchery lies in drinking the wine that makes one drunk. But "wine, in which is debauchery," can also be understood of the wine spoken of in the great Song: "Their wine is the rage of dragons, and the incurable rage of asps" (Deuteronomy 32:33). All who are out of their minds and drunk in their reasoning drink this wine, and it is full of debauchery. Set against that wine, which makes drunk and in which is debauchery, is its opposite: the one who has been filled with spirit and receives all of what is more divine that he has room for. We have often observed that the word "spirit," written without any addition, is said of the better; and that is what it means here too.

"Speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord" (Ephesians 5:19). Origen says: Hymns proclaim the power and divinity of God, and the one who has knowledge of how to speak of God would be in spiritual hymns. Perhaps the one who treats of what is to be done, and of the things one must carry out through our body as through an instrument, a kind of psaltery, is in spiritual psalms; and the one who, on the other hand, studies nature, the order of the world and the rest of what was made, is in spiritual songs. And we must sing in keeping with the study of nature, and make melody in keeping with the account of conduct, to the Lord, sincerely disposed toward what is said; for this is what it is to make melody and sing in the heart to the Lord.

"Always giving thanks for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father" (Ephesians 5:20). In the First Letter to the Thessalonians, too, he says, "Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything" (1 Thessalonians 5:16-18). This commandment will be kept by the one who has understood that providence reaches even to the five sparrows sold for two pennies, not one of which falls into a snare without the Father in heaven. To give thanks in everything is also to give thanks for everything. So we must give thanks for hardships too, since these are also among the things for which we must give thanks. And just as a person in the world must give thanks for sharing in the world, for gazing at its beauty, and for seeing how many and what kind of things have come to be for the sake of the rational creature, so too we must give thanks for particular things. Whoever gives thanks to God and the Father must give thanks in the mediator between God and humankind, so that we do what is written: give thanks in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father.

"Submitting," he says, "to one another in the fear of Christ" (Ephesians 5:21). This tears down entirely the love of ruling and of being first. For this commandment is given to all: "For though I am free from all, I made myself a slave to all, that I might win all" (1 Corinthians 9:19). And the commandment that says, "Serve one another," orders the same (Galatians 5:13). That is why the apostles, through love, served the churches as slaves, ministering and serving the salvation of human beings. The Savior himself took the form of a slave, not so much for any other reason as to serve his disciples as a slave, so that once he even poured water into the basin and washed the disciples' feet (John 13:5). And the one who has understood, "Whoever wishes to be great among you shall be the slave of all," submits by serving those whom he ought.

It is possible, however, for one who serves, and who in his service does what is suited to those he serves, to seem not to submit. This happens when those being served, not knowing what is good for them, order those who want to serve them to do things that are not suited to them. Yet even then the one who acts for their good both serves and submits to the need of the one he serves, because of the fear that, according to the word of God, is free of passion and makes us blessed. title: Wives and husbands as church and Christ; spots; children (Eph 5:21–6:3)
english: is what is meant by "in the fear of Christ."

"Wives, be subject to your own husbands as to the Lord; for the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ also is the head of the church" (Ephesians 5:22-23). This saying wants every union of husband and wife to be a symbol of Christ and the church. The husband, if he orders the life of the marriage by reason, imitates Christ, the bridegroom of the church; the wife, if she lives with her husband as she should, strives to match the church's (if I may put it so) shared life with Christ. For so the husband will be the head of the wife, just as Christ is of the church. But if husband and wife are not joined to each other in this way, it could not be said of them that this man is the head of his wife as Christ also is of the church. So let each husband make it his ambition to be toward his wife as Christ is toward the church, and each wife toward her husband as the church is toward Christ. Let the husband think and do all that belongs to Christ, and the wife all that belongs to the church.

"But as the church is subject to Christ, so also wives to their husbands in everything" (Ephesians 5:24). Origen says: If wives must be subject to their husbands in the way the church is subject to Christ, then wives will have to live holy lives, free of passion and without sin, as they are subject to their husbands, just as the church is subject to Christ while living a holy life, free of passion and without sin.

"That he might present the church to himself in glory, having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that it might be holy and blameless" (Ephesians 5:27). Spots are things like the freckles that form on the body, dark patches, white blotches and warts; once these are taken away, a woman would be more beautiful. Let us understand that corresponding things form on the soul too, and it belongs to no one but the Word to take them away, "that he might present to himself," it says, his own bride, "having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she might be holy and blameless." Wrinkles are a sign of old age. So if someone kept bearing traces of the old self and was not always being renewed, he might be said to be wrinkled in his soul.

"For this a man shall leave father and mother, and the two shall become one flesh" (Ephesians 5:31). We should note, as we have done elsewhere, that the writers of the New Testament often do not set out the old Scripture in its exact words. On this point Genesis has: "For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh" (Genesis 2:24). But here, in place of "for this reason," Paul has put "for this"; and he has left out the "his" that comes after "father" and the second "his" that comes after "mother," as well as "and be joined to his wife."

"Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is just. 'Honor your father and mother'—which is the first commandment with a promise—'that it may be well with you, and you will live long on the earth'" (Ephesians 6:1-3). Origen says: The text is ambiguous. Either children must obey parents who are in the Lord, or children must obey their parents in the Lord. And neither reading should be rejected. Parents in the Lord, as Paul was to the Corinthians, must be obeyed; and parents according to the flesh must be obeyed too, but in the Lord, when they command nothing contrary to the Lord's will. In either sense, obeying is just.

At the same time, you will note this against the heterodox who separate a just God from a good one: to the disciples of the one they call "the good," he gives what they would call a command of the other God, if indeed that other God is the just one; and Paul says that it is just for children to obey their parents in the Lord, or to obey their parents in the Lord. The text is taken from Exodus, which reads: "Honor your father and your mother, that it may be well with you, and that you may live long on the land which the Lord your God gives you" (Exodus 20:12). Here too, as he sets out the words, the apostle has left out the "your" after "mother"; in place of "and that you may live long" he has put "and you will live long"; and after "on the earth" he has left out "which the Lord your God gives you." Now this commandment is the fifth of the Ten Commandments. So we must ask how to take "which is the first commandment," when the first commandment given is, "You shall have no other gods besides me" (Exodus 20:3).
